Among the listed proteins, COL18A1 is particularly relevant to arrhythmia because atrial and ventricular arrhythmias are strongly influenced by structural remodeling, microvascular integrity, and extracellular matrix signaling. Its anti-angiogenic activity suggests a potential role in regulating myocardial vascularization and tissue repair. Excessive inhibition of endothelial proliferation or vascular endothelial growth factor A signaling could impair adaptive angiogenesis in stressed myocardium, thereby promoting ischemia, fibrosis, and heterogeneous conduction, all of which are established substrates for arrhythmogenesis. In addition, its integrin-dependent effects on endothelial migration imply broader consequences for matrix-cell interactions that can influence cardiac remodeling. Because arrhythmia frequently emerges in the setting of fibrosis, chamber remodeling, and impaired perfusion, COL18A1 stands out as a plausible modifier of the myocardial microenvironment that may indirectly favor arrhythmic disease mechanisms.[PubMed:9459295](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9459295) [PubMed:11257123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11257123) 

In a related manner, growth factor regulation may represent another route through which extracellular matrix-associated biology intersects with arrhythmia susceptibility. FGFBP1 is highly relevant to arrhythmia because fibroblast growth factor signaling, extracellular signal-regulated kinase pathway activation, and angiogenic remodeling are central components of cardiac stress responses. Its ability to promote cell survival, proliferation, migration, and angiogenesis suggests that it may influence myocardial repair and remodeling after injury. These processes are closely tied to arrhythmia susceptibility: maladaptive growth signaling can contribute to fibrosis, altered cell-cell coupling, and chamber remodeling, while abnormal angiogenic responses may create regional heterogeneity in perfusion and electrophysiological stability. The involvement of integrin-mediated fibroblast growth factor 2 signaling is also notable, as integrin-extracellular matrix signaling regulates mechanotransduction in the heart and may affect substrate formation for atrial or ventricular arrhythmias. Therefore, FGFBP1 stands out as a candidate linking growth factor signaling and structural remodeling to arrhythmic risk.[PubMed:8663044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8663044) [PubMed:28302677](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28302677) [PubMed:1721615](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1721615) [PubMed:3732516](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3732516) [PubMed:3964259](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3964259) [PubMed:23469107](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23469107) [PubMed:29501879](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29501879) 

Another potentially important dimension is inflammation, which often interacts with structural remodeling in arrhythmogenic states. PLA2G2A is arguably one of the strongest arrhythmia-relevant proteins in this list because inflammation and lipid mediator signaling are major drivers of electrical instability in the heart. By liberating arachidonate and promoting downstream eicosanoid production, PLA2G2A may enhance inflammatory signaling pathways that alter ion channel behavior, calcium handling, gap junction integrity, and fibrotic remodeling, each of which can promote atrial or ventricular arrhythmias. Its role in sterile inflammation is particularly important, as myocardial injury and systemic inflammatory states are well-recognized triggers for arrhythmogenesis. Moreover, its integrin-activating functions and effects on cell proliferation suggest additional influence on extracellular matrix remodeling and tissue repair, processes that can generate conduction heterogeneity. Thus, PLA2G2A links inflammation, bioactive lipid production, and remodeling, making it highly pertinent to arrhythmic disease mechanisms.[PubMed:10358193](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10358193) [PubMed:11694541](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11694541) [PubMed:8425615](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8425615) [PubMed:27292189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27292189) 

Moving from inflammatory signaling to systemic metabolic influences, APOC1 may be relevant to arrhythmia primarily through metabolic and vascular mechanisms. Disturbances in lipoprotein handling, fatty acid uptake, and cholesterol transport can contribute to atherosclerosis, coronary microvascular dysfunction, and systemic metabolic stress, all of which increase the risk of atrial and ventricular arrhythmias. Its ability to alter free fatty acid handling is especially noteworthy because myocardial electrophysiology is sensitive to lipid metabolic state; excess circulating fatty acids and abnormal intracellular lipid processing can promote oxidative stress, inflammation, and cellular dysfunction. In addition, cholesteryl ester transfer protein-related lipid imbalance may influence broader cardiometabolic risk, indirectly shaping arrhythmia susceptibility through ischemic heart disease and structural remodeling. Although APOC1 is not a canonical ion-channel gene, it stands out as a plausible upstream metabolic contributor to arrhythmogenic substrate formation.

The next proteins further reinforce the broader theme of extracellular matrix organization. DCN (decorin) is notable because regulation of fibril formation is directly relevant to extracellular matrix organization and fibrosis, which are among the most important structural substrates for arrhythmia. Even though the functional description provided here is brief, altered collagen fibrillogenesis can change myocardial stiffness, disrupt anisotropic conduction, and promote reentry by separating cardiomyocyte bundles with fibrotic tissue. In atrial fibrillation especially, extracellular matrix remodeling is a central pathogenic mechanism. Therefore, a protein that influences fibril formation may have meaningful implications for arrhythmia through effects on cardiac fibrosis and tissue architecture, even if the current annotation does not explicitly mention the heart.

Along similar lines, COL6A3 is potentially relevant to arrhythmia because cell-binding extracellular matrix proteins help regulate cell adhesion, mechanotransduction, and tissue organization. In the myocardium, altered matrix-cell interactions can influence fibroblast activation, cardiomyocyte coupling, and structural remodeling. These changes are important in the development of conduction abnormalities and reentrant arrhythmias. Although the provided annotation is limited, the fact that COL6A3 functions as a cell-binding matrix protein suggests a role in the extracellular scaffold that shapes the electrical and mechanical properties of cardiac tissue. This makes it a plausible contributor to arrhythmia susceptibility, particularly in fibrotic or remodeled hearts.

By comparison, the remaining proteins appear to have more indirect or less well-defined links to arrhythmia within the scope of the provided annotations. GSN appears less directly connected to arrhythmia than the remodeling- and inflammation-related proteins above, but it may still have indirect relevance through regulation of reparative or inflammatory cell populations. Stem and progenitor cell behavior can influence post-injury healing, inflammatory responses, and fibrosis, all of which affect arrhythmia substrate formation. However, based on the functions provided here, the link is comparatively weaker and more speculative than for proteins involved in angiogenesis, extracellular matrix remodeling, or inflammatory lipid signaling.[PubMed:7694679](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7694679) 

Finally, C1QA has only a limited arrhythmia connection based on the function listed here. Its relevance would most likely be indirect, through infection- or immune-mediated cardiac injury. Viral and immune activation can contribute to myocarditis, fibrosis, and subsequent arrhythmias, but the annotation provided focuses specifically on Epstein-Barr virus receptor activity rather than broader complement or inflammatory functions. Therefore, while infection-related cardiac inflammation can certainly be arrhythmogenic, the evidence from the supplied function is not as compelling as for the other highlighted proteins.

### structural constituent of muscle (GO:0008307) 

The pathway termed structural constituent of muscle refers to the molecular function of proteins that physically support the architecture, mechanical stability, and force-transmitting capacity of muscle fibers. These molecules are integral components of the contractile apparatus, the sarcomere, the cytoskeleton, the cell membrane-associated costamere system, and the intercellular junctional structures that preserve tissue integrity during repeated cycles of contraction and relaxation. In striated muscle, including cardiac muscle, structural proteins such as actin-associated elements, myosin-associated elements, titin, desmin, dystrophin-associated proteins, and proteins of the intercalated disc maintain alignment of myofibrils, distribute mechanical stress, and couple mechanical force generation to neighboring cells and to the extracellular matrix. In the heart, this structural network is especially important because cardiomyocytes must withstand lifelong rhythmic contraction while preserving electrical continuity and synchronized excitation. Thus, the structural constituent of muscle pathway is relevant not only to mechanical performance, but also to mechanoelectrical coupling, cellular survival, tissue remodeling, and maintenance of normal impulse propagation.

With this functional context in mind, the potential relationship between this pathway and arrhythmia can be considered in a biologically coherent manner. No relevant publications were provided for direct citation-based analysis, but the biological relationship between the structural constituent of muscle pathway and arrhythmia is supported by established cardiac pathophysiology. Arrhythmia frequently emerges when the structural framework of cardiac muscle is disrupted, because defects in sarcomeric, cytoskeletal, membrane-anchoring, or intercellular junctional proteins can weaken cardiomyocyte integrity, alter force transmission, and provoke myocardial injury, fibrosis, and chamber remodeling. These structural changes may create a heterogeneous substrate for abnormal impulse generation and conduction by separating cardiomyocytes, disturbing the architecture of the intercalated disc, and modifying the spatial organization of ion channels and gap junctions. In addition, impaired mechanical stability may activate stress signaling, calcium-handling abnormalities, and mechanoelectrical feedback mechanisms that could further increase susceptibility to triggered activity and reentry. Therefore, although this pathway is defined in terms of muscle structural integrity, in the heart it appears directly relevant to arrhythmia because preservation of muscle structure is closely linked to preservation of coordinated electrical activation. When structural constituent proteins are altered by inherited variation, acquired injury, or maladaptive remodeling, the resulting electromechanical instability may promote both atrial and ventricular arrhythmia.

Building on this biological rationale, the enrichment results provide a more focused quantitative perspective on the pathway. There were 5 arrhythmia-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway termed structural constituent of muscle. This enrichment indicates that a focused set of 5 proteins converges on a molecular function directly related to muscle fiber architecture, mechanical stability, force transmission, and preservation of tissue integrity during repeated contraction and relaxation, all of which are highly relevant to the pathophysiology of arrhythmia in cardiac tissue. In the heart, where rhythmic contraction must be sustained continuously, disruption of even a small structural module such as this 5-protein set may have disproportionate biological consequences by impairing myofibrillar alignment, weakening mechanical coupling, altering intercellular junctional stability, and disturbing the relationship between mechanical stress and electrical impulse propagation. Because this pathway explicitly connects structural support with mechanical performance, cellular survival, tissue remodeling, and maintenance of normal impulse conduction, the enrichment of these 5 proteins provides quantitative evidence that muscle structural integrity is a biologically meaningful component of arrhythmia-associated molecular organization.

KRT19 is potentially relevant to arrhythmia because it participates in the structural organization of striated muscle and, together with KRT8, contributes to coupling the contractile apparatus to dystrophin at costameres. Although KRT19 is not a canonical ion-channel or desmosomal arrhythmia gene, this function is notable because cardiomyocyte electrical stability depends strongly on preserved cytoarchitecture and mechanical integrity. Costameres are critical sites that transmit force between the sarcomere and the cell membrane, and disruption of dystrophin-associated mechanical coupling is well known to promote cardiomyopathy, membrane instability, maladaptive remodeling, and secondary arrhythmogenesis. Therefore, proteins such as KRT19 that support myofiber organization and dystrophin-linked structural continuity may have an indirect but biologically meaningful connection to arrhythmia, particularly in disease settings where cytoskeletal disorganization, mechanical stress, or cardiomyopathic remodeling create an arrhythmogenic substrate.

### myofibril assembly (GO:0030239) 

Myofibril assembly is the developmental and homeostatic process by which cardiomyocytes build the highly ordered contractile apparatus of striated muscle. This process includes the stepwise organization of actin-containing thin filaments, myosin-containing thick filaments, titin-based elastic scaffolds, and the formation and alignment of sarcomeres into mature myofibrils. In the heart, proper myofibril assembly is essential not only for force generation but also for preservation of cellular architecture, mechanical coupling between neighboring cardiomyocytes, and coordinated electromechanical behavior of the myocardium. Because the contractile cytoskeleton is physically and functionally linked to intercalated discs, costameres, ion channel positioning, calcium handling systems, and mechanoresponsive signaling pathways, disturbances in myofibril assembly can alter myocardial structure and function at multiple levels. Defects in this pathway may therefore contribute to cardiomyocyte disorganization, impaired contractility, abnormal ventricular remodeling, fibrosis, and altered conduction properties, all of which are recognized substrates for arrhythmia.

Against this biological background, the potential relevance of this pathway to arrhythmia can be considered in a cautious but mechanistically coherent manner. Although no specific publications were provided for direct citation, the biological relationship between myofibril assembly and arrhythmia is strongly supported by established cardiac pathophysiology. In the heart, accurate assembly of myofibrils is required for normal sarcomere formation, mechanical stability, and synchronization of contraction across the myocardium. When myofibril assembly is impaired, cardiomyocytes may develop sarcomeric disarray, abnormal force transmission, and defective coupling to the membrane systems that regulate calcium cycling and electrical propagation. These abnormalities can promote electrophysiological instability through several mechanisms, including disturbed intracellular calcium homeostasis, mechanoelectrical feedback, maladaptive hypertrophic remodeling, and the development of fibrosis and chamber dilation. In addition, disruption of the structural continuity between the contractile apparatus and intercellular junctions can impair conduction and increase spatial heterogeneity of excitation, thereby creating a substrate for reentrant and triggered arrhythmias. Accordingly, genes that govern sarcomere formation and myofibril organization are frequently implicated in inherited cardiomyopathies, and these cardiomyopathies are well known to carry increased arrhythmia risk. Thus, even in the absence of pathway-specific publications in the provided list, myofibril assembly appears mechanistically relevant to arrhythmia because it helps establish and maintain the structural framework that underlies normal cardiac electrical and mechanical integration.

Consistent with this framework, the enrichment results provide a quantitative basis for considering this pathway further. There were 8 arrhythmia-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of myofibril assembly, a process that governs the ordered construction of thin filaments, thick filaments, titin-based scaffolds, and sarcomeres required for stable cardiomyocyte architecture and synchronized myocardial contraction. Given that this pathway directly connects force generation with cellular alignment, mechanical coupling, calcium handling, and conduction-related structural integrity, enrichment of 8 proteins in this functional category supports a quantitatively defined link between contractile apparatus organization and arrhythmia susceptibility, particularly through mechanisms involving impaired electromechanical coordination, ventricular remodeling, and fibrosis. To extend the interpretation from pathway-level enrichment to individual candidates, the significantly enriched proteins are discussed below in the same analytical context. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

Among the listed proteins, EDN1 has one of the clearest and most biologically plausible connections to arrhythmia. Endothelin-1 is a major vasoactive and pro-remodeling mediator, and its signaling is highly relevant to cardiovascular electrophysiology because it can influence vascular tone, intracellular calcium handling, hypertrophic signaling, and structural remodeling. The reported activation of RHOA/ROCK and NFATC3 pathways is especially notable, as these pathways are broadly associated with maladaptive cardiovascular remodeling, including hypertrophy and fibrosis-like phenotypes that create an arrhythmogenic substrate. Although the cited functional description emphasizes mesangial and vascular smooth muscle contexts, the same signaling logic is highly relevant to the heart, where endothelin signaling has been implicated in electrical instability, altered conduction, and remodeling-associated susceptibility to atrial and ventricular arrhythmias. Thus, EDN1 stands out as a strong candidate for arrhythmia relevance because it links neurohumoral signaling to hypertrophic and cytoskeletal transcriptional programs that can secondarily disturb cardiac rhythm.[PubMed:16293765](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16293765) [PubMed:20495147](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20495147) [PubMed:21525433](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21525433) 

In a related but somewhat more stromal and remodeling-oriented context, PDGFRA may also be relevant to arrhythmia biology. PDGFRA is highly relevant to arrhythmia primarily through its roles in mesenchymal biology, tissue remodeling, and calcium-linked signal transduction. Its ability to activate PLCG1, increase inositol trisphosphate production, mobilize cytosolic Ca2+, and stimulate PKC suggests a potential interface with cellular excitability and calcium-dependent stress signaling, both central to arrhythmogenesis. More importantly, PDGFRA is a key regulator of proliferation, migration, and differentiation in mesenchymal-lineage cells, making it mechanistically relevant to cardiac fibroblast activation and fibrotic remodeling, which are major determinants of conduction heterogeneity and re-entry. In disease settings, excessive PDGF signaling has been associated with structural remodeling and fibrosis in the cardiovascular system; therefore, even though the functional annotation here is broad and developmental, PDGFRA stands out as a plausible arrhythmia-associated protein because it can contribute to the formation of an arrhythmogenic substrate through pro-survival, pro-migratory, and pro-remodeling signaling cascades.

Shifting from signaling mediators to structural regulators, LMOD1 may be considered as a candidate linked more indirectly through cytoskeletal organization. LMOD1 is potentially relevant to arrhythmia because it directly regulates actin filament assembly and contractile apparatus integrity. Although the cited evidence specifically concerns visceral smooth muscle, proteins that control actin dynamics often have broader implications for muscle-cell architecture and mechanotransduction. In the heart, disruption of cytoskeletal organization can alter force transmission, cellular shape, and mechano-electric coupling, all of which may influence arrhythmia susceptibility indirectly. LMOD1 therefore stands out as a structural and contractility-associated candidate whose dysfunction could contribute to abnormal muscle mechanics and remodeling states that favor electrical instability, even if the current annotation does not provide direct cardiac evidence.[PubMed:28292896](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28292896) 

Along similar structural lines, KRT19 may be of interest because of its potential role in linking the contractile apparatus to membrane-associated support systems. KRT19 is of interest because it participates in structural coupling within striated muscle, specifically at costameres that mechanically connect the contractile apparatus to the cell membrane-associated dystrophin complex. This type of cytoskeletal anchoring is important for maintaining tissue integrity during repeated contraction. In the context of arrhythmia, defects in structural proteins and membrane-cytoskeleton coupling can predispose to cardiomyopathic remodeling, impaired force transmission, and secondary conduction abnormalities. While KRT19 is not a canonical arrhythmia gene, its role in organizing myofibers and linking to dystrophin suggests a plausible connection to arrhythmogenic disease mechanisms through structural fragility and altered mechano-electric interactions in muscle tissue.

Continuing within the sarcomeric theme, MYBPC1 may represent another indirectly relevant component of contractile system integrity. MYBPC1 is noteworthy because myosin-binding proteins are central regulators of sarcomeric organization and contractile performance. Although MYBPC1 is more strongly associated with skeletal muscle than with the canonical cardiac myosin-binding protein family member MYBPC3, its annotated role in muscular differentiation and function suggests potential relevance to muscle structural integrity. In arrhythmia biology, sarcomeric dysfunction can promote chamber remodeling, mechanical stress, and downstream electrophysiological disturbance. Therefore, MYBPC1 may represent an indirect arrhythmia-relevant candidate, particularly if altered expression reflects a broader myopathic or remodeling program affecting electrically active muscle tissue.

Finally, MYOM3 further supports the possibility that proteins involved in preserving myofibrillar ultrastructure could contribute to arrhythmia susceptibility through remodeling-related mechanisms. MYOM3 is potentially relevant to arrhythmia because it contributes to myofibrillar structural organization by linking the cytoskeleton to the M-disk. This function is important for preserving sarcomere alignment and mechanical stability in striated muscle. Structural disorganization of the contractile apparatus can facilitate cardiomyopathic remodeling, which is a well-established substrate for arrhythmia through fibrosis, chamber dilation, and altered conduction. Although the current annotation does not directly implicate MYOM3 in cardiac electrophysiology, its role in maintaining muscle ultrastructure makes it a plausible modifier of arrhythmia risk in disorders characterized by myofibrillar instability.

### Diseases of glycosylation (REAC:R-HSA-3781865) 

Diseases of glycosylation comprise a heterogeneous group of inherited or acquired disorders in which the enzymatic assembly, processing, transfer, or remodeling of carbohydrate chains on proteins and lipids is impaired. Glycosylation is a fundamental post translational modification required for correct protein folding, intracellular trafficking, membrane targeting, molecular stability, ligand recognition, and cell to cell communication. In the cardiovascular system, glycosylation is essential for the maturation and function of ion channels, transporters, gap junction proteins, adhesion molecules, receptors, and extracellular matrix components that collectively govern cardiac excitability, impulse propagation, structural integrity, and autonomic responsiveness. Disturbance of glycosylation can therefore alter the abundance, localization, and biophysical behavior of membrane proteins that regulate depolarization and repolarization, impair electrical coupling between cardiomyocytes, and promote myocardial remodeling. From a mechanistic perspective, this pathway is relevant to arrhythmia because defective glycosylation may influence sodium channels, potassium channels, calcium handling proteins, and connexins, thereby creating substrates for conduction slowing, triggered activity, and repolarization instability. In addition, systemic diseases of glycosylation may involve multisystem metabolic and structural abnormalities that secondarily affect the heart, including cardiomyopathy and conduction system disease, both of which increase susceptibility to arrhythmia.

Building on this biological framework, the current evidence base provided for this pathway remains limited and should therefore be interpreted cautiously. No relevant publications were provided in the input list, so a publication based pathway specific synthesis cannot be performed from the supplied evidence. Nevertheless, based on established biological principles, diseases of glycosylation are plausibly related to arrhythmia because glycosylation is required for the normal biosynthesis and surface expression of many cardiac membrane proteins that determine impulse generation and propagation. When glycosylation is defective, ion channels may be misfolded, retained within intracellular compartments, or displayed at the cell surface with altered gating properties, leading to abnormalities of cardiac depolarization or repolarization. Similarly, impaired glycosylation of gap junction proteins can reduce intercellular electrical coupling and favor conduction heterogeneity, while altered glycosylation of receptors and extracellular matrix proteins may contribute to autonomic imbalance and structural remodeling that further destabilize cardiac rhythm. In patients with systemic diseases of glycosylation, these molecular defects may coexist with cardiomyopathy or conduction system involvement, thereby increasing the likelihood of atrial arrhythmia, ventricular arrhythmia, or bradyarrhythmic presentations. However, because no citations were supplied, the strength and specificity of the association for this particular pathway in arrhythmia cannot be attributed to the provided literature and should be interpreted as a mechanistic inference rather than a direct evidence based conclusion.

Consistent with this tentative mechanistic interpretation, the enrichment results suggest that this pathway captures a nontrivial subset of arrhythmia associated biology. There were 20 arrhythmia-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway “Diseases of glycosylation comprise a heterogeneous group of inherited or acquired disorders in which the enzymatic assembly, processing, transfer, or remodeling of carbohydrate chains on proteins and lipids is impaired. Glycosylation is a fundamental post translational modification required for correct protein folding, intracellular trafficking, membrane targeting, molecular stability, ligand recognition, and cell to cell communication. In the cardiovascular system, glycosylation is essential for the maturation and function of ion channels, transporters, gap junction proteins, adhesion molecules, receptors, and extracellular matrix components that collectively govern cardiac excitability, impulse propagation, structural integrity, and autonomic responsiveness. Disturbance of glycosylation can therefore alter the abundance, localization, and biophysical behavior of membrane proteins that regulate depolarization and repolarization, impair electrical coupling between cardiomyocytes, and promote myocardial remodeling. From a mechanistic perspective, this pathway is relevant to arrhythmia because defective glycosylation may influence sodium channels, potassium channels, calcium handling proteins, and connexins, thereby creating substrates for conduction slowing, triggered activity, and repolarization instability. In addition, systemic diseases of glycosylation may involve multisystem metabolic and structural abnormalities that secondarily affect the heart, including cardiomyopathy and conduction system disease, both of which increase susceptibility to arrhythmia.” This enrichment involves a total of 20 proteins, indicating a quantitatively substantial functional module linking altered carbohydrate chain biology to arrhythmia susceptibility through effects on membrane protein maturation, electrical conduction, repolarization control, and myocardial structural remodeling. Among the listed proteins, NOTCH3 stands out as one of the most plausibly relevant to arrhythmia because Notch signaling is a major developmental and homeostatic pathway that can influence cardiovascular cell fate, tissue remodeling, and survival. In the heart, disturbances in differentiation, proliferation, and apoptosis are highly relevant to arrhythmogenic substrates because they can alter myocardial architecture, promote fibrosis, and disrupt electrical coupling. Even though the annotation provided does not describe a direct electrophysiological role, dysregulated NOTCH3 signaling could reasonably contribute to arrhythmia through structural remodeling of the myocardium or vasculature, with secondary effects on conduction heterogeneity. This is particularly important because arrhythmias often arise not only from ion-channel defects but also from maladaptive changes in cardiac tissue organization and cell signaling networks.[PubMed:15350543](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15350543) 

In a related but distinct way, inflammatory pathway components may also shape arrhythmia susceptibility through myocardial injury and remodeling. CFP is notable because it links innate immunity and inflammatory amplification to potential arrhythmia mechanisms. Complement activation can promote tissue injury, endothelial dysfunction, and inflammatory remodeling, all of which are recognized contributors to atrial and ventricular arrhythmogenesis. By stabilizing alternative pathway convertases and preserving C3b, CFP may intensify inflammatory responses. In a cardiac context, excessive complement activity could contribute to myocardial injury, fibrosis, and conduction abnormalities, thereby creating a substrate for arrhythmia. Although the provided annotation does not establish a direct causal role in cardiac rhythm disorders, the biological connection between inflammation and arrhythmia makes CFP a meaningful candidate of interest.[PubMed:28264884](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28264884) 

Extending this theme of inflammation and tissue remodeling, extracellular matrix associated proteins may provide additional indirect links to arrhythmogenic remodeling. SPON2 is of potential relevance to arrhythmia primarily through inflammation and extracellular matrix biology. Its role as an opsonin and innate immune mediator suggests that it may participate in inflammatory signaling and tissue responses to infection or sterile injury. Since inflammatory activation is increasingly recognized as an important driver of atrial remodeling, fibrosis, and electrical instability, SPON2 may be indirectly connected to arrhythmogenesis. In addition, as an extracellular matrix-associated adhesion protein, SPON2 could influence cell-matrix interactions that affect tissue integrity and remodeling. These processes are important because altered extracellular matrix composition can slow conduction and facilitate reentry, a central mechanism in many arrhythmias.

A conceptually similar but somewhat broader possibility applies to SPON1, which may connect adhesion biology with autonomic and vascular influences on rhythm. SPON1 is potentially relevant because of its roles in cell adhesion, neurite outgrowth, and vascular smooth muscle biology. Arrhythmia can be influenced not only by cardiomyocyte-intrinsic abnormalities but also by autonomic innervation and vascular remodeling. A protein involved in axonal growth and guidance may be relevant to cardiac autonomic patterning, which can modulate excitability and trigger arrhythmias. Its association with vascular smooth muscle cells may also be important, as vascular pathology can contribute indirectly to myocardial ischemia or structural remodeling, both of which increase arrhythmia susceptibility. While the current annotation does not provide direct cardiac evidence, SPON1 represents a biologically plausible modifier of arrhythmia-related tissue environments.

By comparison, some proteins in the enriched set appear to have a weaker or more context dependent relationship with arrhythmia. MUC13 is not an obvious canonical arrhythmia gene, but it may still be relevant at a systems level because transmembrane mucins can modulate cell signaling and inflammatory responses. If expressed in cardiovascular or immune-associated contexts, altered MUC13 signaling could contribute indirectly to arrhythmia through inflammatory or remodeling pathways. However, based on the function provided, the evidence connecting MUC13 to arrhythmia is weaker than for proteins involved in developmental signaling, complement activation, or extracellular matrix regulation. Therefore, MUC13 should be considered a lower-priority candidate whose relevance would likely depend on tissue-specific expression and disease context.

A similarly cautious interpretation is appropriate for GPC5, although its biology may still intersect with remodeling related mechanisms. GPC5 may be relevant to arrhythmia because heparan sulfate proteoglycans regulate growth factor signaling, cell-cell communication, and extracellular interactions. In the heart, these processes can influence development, fibrosis, and responses to injury. Although the supplied annotation is brief, cell-surface proteoglycans often act as modulators of signaling pathways that affect structural remodeling, which is a major determinant of arrhythmia susceptibility. Nevertheless, compared with NOTCH3 or CFP, the direct mechanistic link from the provided information is less compelling, so GPC5 should be viewed as a plausible but less strongly prioritized candidate.

The uncertainty becomes greater for proteins with limited functional annotation in the supplied dataset. ADAMTSL2 cannot be strongly interpreted from the present dataset because no functional annotation was supplied. However, proteins in the ADAMTS-like family are often associated with extracellular matrix organization, and extracellular matrix remodeling is highly relevant to arrhythmia because fibrosis and altered tissue mechanics can impair conduction and promote reentry. In the absence of a specific function or citation in the input, ADAMTSL2 should be regarded as an unresolved candidate rather than a highlighted arrhythmia-associated protein.

Returning more directly to the central pathway theme, glycosylation enzymes themselves may offer mechanistic plausibility, although the current annotations remain indirect. B4GALT1 is more likely to have an indirect than a direct relationship with arrhythmia. Its broader role in glycoprotein glycosylation could be relevant because glycosylation affects the stability, trafficking, and function of membrane proteins, including receptors and ion channels that are critical for cardiac electrophysiology. Abnormal glycosylation can theoretically alter excitability or intercellular communication. However, based on the provided annotation, the strongest described functions are centered on lactose synthase regulation and general glycoprotein processing rather than a specific cardiovascular pathway. Thus, B4GALT1 is biologically plausible but not among the most compelling proteins in this list for arrhythmia relevance.

Finally, B4GAT1 appears to be the least directly connected to cardiac rhythm regulation within the currently provided functional descriptions. B4GAT1 appears to have limited direct relevance to arrhythmia based on the function provided. Its principal role in mucin-type O-glycan biosynthesis in digestive organs suggests a tissue context that is not immediately connected to cardiac rhythm regulation. Although glycosylation pathways can broadly influence protein function and signaling, there is insufficient information here to prioritize B4GAT1 as a meaningful arrhythmia-related candidate. Relative to proteins involved in developmental signaling, immunity, or extracellular matrix interactions, B4GAT1 is less likely to represent a major mechanistic link.

### regulation of receptor binding (GO:1900120) 

Regulation of receptor binding refers to any biological process that alters whether, how strongly, how often, or how long a ligand, protein, peptide, lipid mediator, ion, extracellular matrix component, or other signaling molecule binds to its cognate receptor. This pathway is fundamental to cellular communication because receptor binding is the initiating event for many downstream signaling cascades that control excitability, contraction, metabolism, inflammation, growth, and cell survival. Regulation can occur at multiple levels, including changes in ligand availability, post-translational modification of receptors or ligands, receptor density at the cell surface, receptor conformation, competition by agonists or antagonists, co-receptor interactions, extracellular matrix sequestration of ligands, and receptor desensitization or internalization. In the cardiovascular system, regulation of receptor binding is especially important because cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, autonomic neurons, and inflammatory cells all rely on tightly controlled receptor-mediated signaling to maintain cardiac rhythm and conduction. Receptors for catecholamines, acetylcholine, angiotensin, endothelin, adenosine, cytokines, and growth factors influence ion channel activity, intracellular calcium handling, action potential duration, conduction velocity, fibrosis, and structural remodeling. Therefore, disturbances in the regulation of receptor binding may plausibly promote either acute electrical instability or chronic substrate formation that predisposes the heart to arrhythmia.  

In this context, the pathway can be viewed as a broad mechanistic framework linking extracellular signaling to downstream electrophysiological and structural consequences. No relevant publications were provided for direct citation-based analysis. Nevertheless, from a mechanistic perspective, regulation of receptor binding appears highly relevant to arrhythmia because abnormal receptor-ligand interactions may alter both the triggers and the substrate required for disordered cardiac rhythm. Excessive binding of sympathetic agonists to adrenergic receptors can increase calcium influx and spontaneous calcium release, thereby favoring delayed afterdepolarization and triggered activity, whereas altered binding of parasympathetic ligands to muscarinic receptors can shorten atrial refractoriness and facilitate reentry. Dysregulated binding at receptors for angiotensin, endothelin, inflammatory mediators, and growth factors may further drive fibrosis, gap junction remodeling, oxidative stress, and heterogeneity of conduction, all of which could help stabilize arrhythmogenic circuits. Conversely, impaired receptor binding may blunt protective signaling pathways, such as those that normally limit excitability, inflammation, or ischemic injury. Because receptor occupancy is determined not only by ligand concentration but also by receptor abundance, affinity, localization, and desensitization state, this pathway provides a unifying framework that links neurohumoral activation, inflammation, structural remodeling, and electrophysiological instability in arrhythmia. However, in the absence of the requested publications, any disease-specific conclusion remains inferential rather than directly supported by the supplied literature.  

Against this mechanistic background, the enrichment results provide a more focused view of the proteins that may contribute to this pathway in the arrhythmia-associated dataset. There were 5 arrhythmia-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of regulation of receptor binding. This functional category is highly relevant to arrhythmia because receptor binding is the first quantitative step in signal transduction, and even small alterations in binding strength, duration, frequency, or receptor occupancy can propagate into measurable changes in ion channel regulation, intracellular calcium flux, conduction velocity, tissue remodeling, and electrical stability. In the cardiovascular context, this pathway connects extracellular signaling to electrophysiological control across multiple cell populations, including cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, autonomic neurons, and inflammatory cells, thereby providing a plausible mechanistic bridge between molecular signaling disturbance and both acute and chronic arrhythmogenic processes. With a total of 5 enriched proteins, the analysis supports a focused but biologically coherent signal, suggesting that dysregulation of receptor-ligand interaction control may contribute materially to the arrhythmia phenotype through effects on excitability, contraction, inflammation, fibrosis, and cell survival. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 5 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is also provided for direct network exploration.

Having outlined the pathway-level interpretation, the following section introduces the individual significant proteins identified in the enrichment analysis. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

MMP9 stands out as the protein with the strongest potential relevance to arrhythmia because its annotated functions converge on extracellular matrix remodeling, vascular wall integrity, and smooth muscle biology, all of which are closely linked to structural heart disease and arrhythmogenic substrate formation. The reported roles of MMP9 in elastic fiber formation, collagen organization, and LOX-dependent cross-linking indicate that it can influence tissue stiffness and matrix architecture, processes that are central to cardiac fibrosis and adverse remodeling. In the arrhythmia context, matrix disorganization and fibrosis promote conduction heterogeneity, slow impulse propagation, and re-entry. Its additional involvement in vascular smooth muscle proliferation through angiotensin signaling is also notable, because activation of the renin-angiotensin system is a well-established driver of myocardial remodeling, inflammation, and atrial as well as ventricular arrhythmogenesis. Although the annotation emphasizes vascular and aortic biology rather than direct electrophysiological regulation, the mechanistic overlap with fibrosis, structural remodeling, and neurohormonal activation makes MMP9 a highly plausible contributor to arrhythmia susceptibility, particularly in settings such as hypertensive heart disease, ischemic remodeling, and atrial fibrillation.[PubMed:27339457](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27339457) [PubMed:18973305](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18973305) [PubMed:19570982](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19570982) [PubMed:23782690](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23782690)   

A related but somewhat more indirect line of reasoning applies to proteins that influence cardiometabolic risk and receptor trafficking rather than extracellular matrix structure itself. PCSK9 is particularly relevant to arrhythmia through indirect but clinically important mechanisms. Its best-established function is the control of LDL receptor abundance and plasma cholesterol homeostasis, which links it strongly to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. This is meaningful for arrhythmia because ischemic heart disease is a major substrate for both atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, and lipid-driven coronary disease can lead to myocardial scar formation, chamber remodeling, and electrical instability. Beyond lipid metabolism, PCSK9 also affects ENaC surface expression and sodium handling, a function that may be relevant to electrolyte balance and volume status, both of which can modulate arrhythmia risk. Its actions on LRP family receptors and cell survival pathways further suggest broader effects on tissue homeostasis. Although the provided citations do not directly connect PCSK9 to cardiac electrophysiology, its central role in cardiometabolic risk, receptor trafficking, and sodium transport makes it an important protein in the broader pathophysiological landscape that predisposes to arrhythmia, especially in coronary artery disease and heart failure.[PubMed:18039658](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18039658) [PubMed:17461796](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17461796) [PubMed:18197702](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18197702) [PubMed:18799458](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18799458) [PubMed:22074827](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22074827) [PubMed:18660751](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18660751)   

Shifting from lipid and receptor trafficking biology to tissue repair and adhesion-related remodeling, ADAM15 is of potential interest for arrhythmia because its functions implicate it in proteolytic remodeling of the extracellular environment, regulation of integrin signaling, and wound-healing responses. These processes are relevant to the development of arrhythmogenic structural substrates after myocardial injury, where altered cell adhesion, matrix turnover, and tissue repair can contribute to fibrosis and conduction abnormalities. The ability of ADAM15 to modulate beta-1 integrin-mediated adhesion and migration, suppress motility on fibronectin, and cleave E-cadherin suggests that it may influence intercellular coupling and tissue organization during remodeling. Its role in pathological neovascularization may also be relevant in ischemic or inflammatory cardiac disease, where vascular remodeling accompanies scar formation. While the current annotation does not provide direct evidence for a cardiac electrophysiological role, ADAM15 stands out as a plausible modifier of post-injury remodeling and fibrotic repair, both of which are mechanistically linked to atrial and ventricular arrhythmias.  

A complementary perspective is provided by proteins more closely associated with systemic metabolism and stress-response signaling. ADIPOQ is relevant to arrhythmia primarily through metabolic and cardioprotective signaling. Activation of AMPK is especially noteworthy, as this pathway is central to cellular energy sensing, mitochondrial homeostasis, and protection from metabolic stress. Because metabolic dysfunction, obesity, diabetes, and systemic inflammation are major contributors to atrial fibrillation and other arrhythmias, an adipokine that modulates AMPK, AKT, and MAPK signaling may influence arrhythmia susceptibility indirectly by shaping myocardial metabolism, survival signaling, and remodeling responses. In addition, adipokine signaling is increasingly recognized as a link between epicardial adipose tissue, inflammation, and atrial substrate formation. Although the annotation is brief and does not include direct citations or explicit arrhythmia-related functions, ADIPOQ remains biologically interesting because disturbances in adiponectin-associated pathways could alter the metabolic milieu that favors electrical and structural remodeling.  

Finally, compared with the preceding candidates, B2M appears to have a more indirect and context-dependent relationship with arrhythmia. B2M appears less directly connected to arrhythmia than the other highlighted proteins, but it may still be relevant in an indirect inflammatory or infectious disease context. The annotated function emphasizes antigen presentation and antiviral immune control, particularly in chronic HIV-1 infection. This could matter for arrhythmia because chronic immune activation, systemic inflammation, and infection-associated cardiomyopathy can all increase the risk of atrial and ventricular rhythm disturbances. However, compared with proteins involved in matrix remodeling, vascular biology, or cardiometabolic regulation, the evidence linking B2M to arrhythmia from the present annotation is relatively weak. Therefore, B2M should be considered a lower-priority candidate whose relevance would likely depend on specific disease settings characterized by inflammation, immune dysregulation, or viral cardiac involvement.

### Arthralgia (HP:0002829) 

Arthralgia refers to joint pain and is a clinical symptom rather than a discrete molecular or electrophysiological pathway. It commonly arises in the setting of inflammatory, autoimmune, infectious, metabolic, degenerative, or drug related conditions. From a biological perspective, joint pain may reflect activation of inflammatory mediators, immune signaling, tissue injury responses, and nociceptive pathways, but the term itself does not define a specific mechanistic cascade that can be directly mapped onto cardiac rhythm regulation. Therefore, in contrast to established arrhythmia related pathways such as ion channel dysfunction, myocardial fibrosis, autonomic imbalance, calcium handling abnormalities, or systemic inflammation, arthralgia should be understood primarily as a symptom that may accompany broader disease states rather than as an independent pathway. 

Consistent with this distinction, the currently provided evidence does not support interpretation of arthralgia as a direct regulator of cardiac electrical activity. Based on the information provided, there are no cited publications linking arthralgia itself to arrhythmia, and arthralgia is not recognized as a direct biological pathway governing cardiac electrical activity. Any potential relationship would be indirect and context dependent, arising only when joint pain occurs as part of a broader systemic disorder that also affects the heart. For example, inflammatory or autoimmune diseases can present with joint pain while simultaneously increasing arrhythmia risk through systemic inflammation, myocardial involvement, autonomic disturbance, or structural remodeling of cardiac tissue; however, in such cases the relevant arrhythmia promoting mechanisms are the underlying inflammatory and cardiac processes rather than arthralgia per se. Because no relevant publications were supplied, there is insufficient evidence to support a direct mechanistic association between this pathway description and arrhythmia.

With that conceptual limitation in mind, the enrichment results are more appropriately interpreted at the level of shared systemic biology rather than as evidence for a symptom specific rhythm pathway. There were 20 arrhythmia-associated proteins included in the function enrichment analysis for the pathway described as arthralgia, which is more accurately interpreted as a clinical symptom of joint pain rather than a discrete mechanistic pathway directly governing cardiac rhythm. In this context, the enrichment signal should be understood cautiously, because the biological meaning is likely to reflect broader processes such as inflammation, immune signaling, tissue injury response, and systemic disease burden that can indirectly influence arrhythmia susceptibility, rather than a single pathway with direct electrophysiological specificity. Given that the analyzed set contains 20 proteins, the resulting functional profile is numerically substantial enough to support network level interpretation, while still emphasizing that the pathway label itself does not represent a canonical arrhythmia mechanism in the same way as ion transport disturbance, calcium handling dysregulation, myocardial fibrosis, autonomic imbalance, or systemic inflammatory activation.

Building on this network level view, the following paragraphs summarize the proteins that appeared most notable in the enrichment output and discuss their possible relevance in a cautious and mechanism oriented manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

ELN is among the most relevant proteins in this list with respect to arrhythmia because abnormalities in elastin biology can contribute to vascular stiffening, altered aortic mechanics, and maladaptive ventricular loading conditions, all of which may indirectly promote atrial or ventricular arrhythmogenesis. Its documented roles in elastic lamina organization, smooth muscle cell differentiation, and maintenance of aortic wall integrity indicate that ELN is central to cardiovascular tissue biomechanics. In addition, its involvement in collagen fibril assembly and extracellular matrix cross-linking suggests that ELN may influence myocardial and vascular remodeling, a major substrate for conduction heterogeneity and arrhythmia. The link to angiotensin-dependent regulation of vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation is also notable, because renin-angiotensin signaling is strongly implicated in fibrosis, structural remodeling, and atrial fibrillation susceptibility. Thus, ELN stands out as a plausible contributor to arrhythmia through extracellular matrix remodeling, vascular dysfunction, and altered electromechanical coupling rather than through direct ion-channel effects.[PubMed:16478991](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16478991) [PubMed:19855011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19855011) [PubMed:20019329](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20019329) [PubMed:26486174](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26486174) [PubMed:26711913](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26711913) [PubMed:28508064](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28508064) [PubMed:26178373](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26178373) [PubMed:26220971](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26220971) [PubMed:26690653](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26690653) [PubMed:17324935](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17324935) [PubMed:23636094](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23636094) 

From extracellular matrix and vascular mechanics, the analysis then shifts toward systemic lipid biology and ischemic remodeling. PCSK9 is highly relevant to arrhythmia primarily through its systemic cardiovascular effects. By controlling LDL receptor degradation and plasma cholesterol homeostasis, PCSK9 contributes to atherosclerotic burden, ischemic heart disease, and ventricular remodeling, which are major substrates for both atrial and ventricular arrhythmias. Chronic dyslipidemia and coronary artery disease can produce myocardial scar, ischemia, and chamber remodeling, each of which increases electrical instability. The reported effects of PCSK9 on ENaC-mediated sodium absorption may also be of interest because altered sodium handling can influence blood pressure and volume status, thereby affecting atrial stretch and arrhythmia susceptibility. Although PCSK9 is not a canonical cardiac electrophysiology gene, it stands out because it connects metabolic risk, vascular disease, and structural heart remodeling, all of which are clinically meaningful drivers of arrhythmogenesis.[PubMed:18039658](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18039658) [PubMed:17461796](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17461796) [PubMed:18197702](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18197702) [PubMed:18799458](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18799458) [PubMed:22074827](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22074827) [PubMed:18660751](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18660751) 

A related but more indirect structural theme emerges with nuclear envelope biology. LMNB2 is of potential interest for arrhythmia because nuclear lamina dysfunction is a well-established mechanism in inherited cardiomyopathies that frequently present with conduction disease and malignant arrhythmias. Although LMNB2 is less directly implicated than LMNA in cardiac disease, its role in maintaining nuclear envelope integrity, chromatin organization, and telomere dynamics suggests that disruption could affect cardiomyocyte survival, mechanotransduction, and transcriptional homeostasis. In the heart, these processes are tightly linked to myocardial remodeling and conduction system integrity. Therefore, LMNB2 may represent a mechanistically plausible arrhythmia-associated factor through nuclear structural instability and secondary cardiomyopathic remodeling, even if the evidence is more indirect than for established ion-channel or sarcomeric genes.[PubMed:28241138](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28241138) 

The next group of proteins further reinforces the possibility that inflammatory remodeling may account for much of the observed enrichment signal. PRTN3 is relevant to arrhythmia because it links inflammation, extracellular matrix degradation, and vascular-endothelial dysfunction, all of which contribute to arrhythmogenic remodeling. Its ability to degrade elastin and several collagen types suggests a role in tissue structural remodeling, while its effects on endothelial integrity and neutrophil migration point to inflammatory vascular injury. Inflammation is increasingly recognized as an important driver of atrial fibrillation and other arrhythmias through promotion of fibrosis, oxidative stress, and altered intercellular signaling. Accordingly, PRTN3 may contribute to an arrhythmogenic substrate indirectly by amplifying inflammatory remodeling and extracellular matrix turnover in cardiovascular tissues.[PubMed:2033050](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2033050) [PubMed:28240246](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28240246) [PubMed:3198760](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3198760) [PubMed:23202369](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23202369) [PubMed:22266279](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22266279) [PubMed:36302784](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36302784) 

Continuing this inflammatory line of interpretation, SPP1 is a notable candidate in the context of arrhythmia because it is an immune and inflammatory mediator, and inflammatory signaling is strongly associated with atrial and ventricular remodeling. A cytokine program characterized by increased IFN-gamma and IL-12 together with reduced IL-10 is consistent with a pro-inflammatory milieu that may favor fibrosis, myocyte stress, and electrical heterogeneity. Although the function provided here does not explicitly mention cardiac tissue, SPP1 is widely linked in cardiovascular biology to remodeling and fibrosis, making it biologically plausible that heightened SPP1-associated immune activity could support arrhythmogenic remodeling, particularly in atrial fibrillation or inflammatory cardiomyopathy settings.

In contrast to these matrix and immune centered candidates, ADA2 may be more relevant through neurohumoral regulation. ADA2 is directly interesting for arrhythmia because adrenergic signaling is a central determinant of cardiac automaticity, conduction, and triggered activity. Although alpha-2 adrenergic receptor signaling is often discussed in the context of sympathetic modulation rather than primary cardiomyocyte depolarization, catecholamine-sensitive G protein pathways can substantially alter heart rate control, autonomic balance, and susceptibility to rhythm disturbances. Dysregulated adrenergic tone is a major precipitant of both supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias. Therefore, ADA2 stands out as a potentially relevant modulator of arrhythmia risk through neurohumoral control mechanisms, even if the supplied description does not specify cardiac tissue-specific effects.

The analysis then returns to immune cell activation as another possible source of indirect arrhythmia relevance. TREM2 is potentially relevant to arrhythmia through immune-cell activation and inflammatory remodeling. Although the description is centered on myeloid biology rather than cardiac electrophysiology, innate immune activation is increasingly recognized as a contributor to atrial fibrillation, myocarditis-associated arrhythmias, and adverse ventricular remodeling. The documented roles in cytokine regulation, phagocytic responses, and activation of inflammatory effector pathways suggest that TREM2-related signaling could influence the inflammatory microenvironment that promotes fibrosis and electrical instability. Its significance is therefore indirect but potentially meaningful, particularly in disease settings where immune activation and tissue remodeling are dominant arrhythmogenic mechanisms.[PubMed:15471863](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15471863) [PubMed:9647200](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9647200) [PubMed:15728241](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15728241) [PubMed:16715077](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16715077) [PubMed:21727189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21727189) [PubMed:17086186](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17086186) [PubMed:18957693](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18957693) [PubMed:18685038](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18685038) [PubMed:25690660](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25690660) [PubMed:21257958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21257958) [PubMed:18691974](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18691974) [PubMed:12569157](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12569157) [PubMed:14969392](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14969392) 

A complementary structural perspective is provided by collagen biology. COL5A1 may be relevant to arrhythmia because fibrillar collagens are major determinants of extracellular matrix architecture, and matrix remodeling is a core mechanism underlying conduction slowing and re-entry. Although the provided annotation is general and does not explicitly describe cardiac disease, altered collagen composition can affect myocardial stiffness, anisotropic conduction, and fibrosis. These changes are particularly important in atrial fibrillation and structural cardiomyopathies. Thus, COL5A1 is best viewed as an indirect but biologically plausible arrhythmia-related factor through its role in connective tissue organization and structural remodeling.

In addition to matrix architecture, systemic mineral regulation may also have indirect electrophysiological implications. PTH1R is potentially relevant to arrhythmia because calcium homeostasis is fundamental to cardiac excitability and contraction. Disturbances in systemic calcium balance can alter action potential properties, triggered activity, and conduction behavior. While the provided function focuses on bone and renal calcium regulation rather than direct cardiac signaling, chronic abnormalities in parathyroid hormone pathways and calcium metabolism are clinically associated with electrophysiologic disturbances. Therefore, PTH1R may have an indirect connection to arrhythmia through systemic calcium handling and downstream effects on myocardial electrical stability.

Finally, the remaining candidate again points toward immune regulation as a possible contextual contributor rather than a direct rhythm determinant. TNFRSF13B is of possible interest because the annotation includes a role in intracellular calcium signaling in T cells and in adaptive immune-cell survival. Although there is no direct evidence here for a cardiac electrophysiologic role, immune dysregulation and calcium-dependent signaling pathways can contribute indirectly to arrhythmogenic inflammation and remodeling. Its relevance to arrhythmia is therefore weaker than that of ELN, PCSK9, or inflammatory extracellular matrix regulators, but it may still be considered in contexts where immune-mediated cardiac injury is suspected.[PubMed:23041287](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23041287) [PubMed:24392163](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24392163) [PubMed:27226539](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27226539) [PubMed:32187542](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32187542) [PubMed:7522304](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7522304)
